data.title: WinWay capacity ramp-up continues
data.description:
ROSY PROSPECTS: AI adoption is an irreversible trend and key clients are projecting aggressive demand heading into next year, the chip testing interface supplier said

WinWay Technology Co (穎崴) yesterday said it is ramping up capacity through next year to meet surging demand, brushing aside concerns over an artificial intelligence (AI) bubble and US chip export curbs.

The Nvidia Corp leadership upheaval surrounding CEO Jensen Huang (黃仁勳) is not expected to derail AI’s progress, the Kaohsiung-based supplier of integrated circuit testing interface and coaxial sockets said.

“AI adoption is widely recognized across industries as an irreversible trend,” WinWay chairman Mark Wang (王嘉煌) said on the sidelines of a media gathering in Taipei.

“Overall, demand for semiconductor testing interfaces remains robust, despite market uncertainty,” Wang said.“Our key customers, particularly AI suppliers, are projecting aggressive demand heading into next year.”

WinWay is accelerating its in-house probe expansion in Taiwan, aiming to ramp up monthly capacity from 9 million units at the end of this year to 24 million by the end of next year in preparation for customers’ next-generation chips slated for 2028 through 2030, Wang said.

The company’s probe products are key components used in coaxial sockets and load boards for wafer and chip testing. High-end coaxial socket capacity is projected to surge 82 percent year-on-year to 38,200 units this year, it said.

WinWay reported that third-quarter revenue surged to NT$4.56 billion (US$138.4 million) from NT$3.52 billion in the previous quarter and NT$1.8 billion in the same period last year.

The company attributed the robust growth to rising demand for advanced process nodes such as 7-nanometer process technology.

About 73 percent of its revenue came from high-end coaxial sockets and vertical probe cards used to test AI and high-performance computing chips, the company said.

With the capacity expansions, WinWay expects revenue to grow by a double-digit percentage next year, Wang said, adding that this year’s sales growth has been capped by capacity constraints.

To keep pace with customer demand, the company plans to establish new offices in Dallas, Texas, and in Phoenix, Arizona next year, he said.

The company’s US expansion aligns with capacity buildouts by key customers, including Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (台積電), King Yuan Electronics Co (京元電子), Amkor Technology Inc, Texas Instruments Inc and Tesla Inc.

WinWay’s net profit in the third quarter surged about 54 percent sequentially to a record-high NT$1.034 billion from NT$672 million. That represented annual growth of 178 percent from NT$372 million.

Earnings per share rose to NT$28.55 from NT$18.7 in the second quarter and NT$10.38 in the third quarter last year.

data.title: Hua Nan upbeat on profit growth
data.description:
OPERATIONS: The financial holding firm is focused on expanding its core banking business, developing non-banking services and boosting cross-selling

Hua Nan Financial Holding Co (華南金控) yesterday said it expects profits to continue growing next year, supported by sustained investment in artificial intelligence (AI), steady loan growth and expanding wealth management and overseas businesses.

The group remains optimistic about Taiwan’s economic prospects, as investment in AI and technology is expected to remain strong, although global trade policies, geopolitical tensions and financial market volatility could create uncertainties, Hua Nan Financial president Hsiao Yu-mei (蕭玉美) told an online earnings conference.

The company would focus on expanding its core banking business, developing non-bank operations and strengthening cross-selling among subsidiaries to sustain earnings growth, she said.

Interest and fee income would benefit from monetary tightening in the US and Taiwan to curb inflation, Hsiao said.

The US Federal Reserve is expected to raise interest rates by 25 basis points next month and possibly again early next year, she said.

Taiwan’s central bank could raise interest rates by 12.5 basis points next month, before keeping them unchanged throughout next year, she added.

The company posted net profit of NT$28.46 billion (US$863.81 million) in the first 10 months, up 26.9 percent from a year earlier and already surpassing its full-year earnings for last year.

Earnings per share reached NT$2.02, a record high.

Hua Nan Commercial Bank Ltd (華南銀行), the group’s main subsidiary, benefited from steady loan growth and an improved deposit and loan mix, lifting net interest income by 12 percent in the first 10 months.

Its wealth management business also gained momentum, with fee income increasing 28.9 percent year-on-year, while revenue from wealth management rose 34 percent.

The number of high-net-worth customers exceeded 3,700, up 83 percent from a year earlier, while assets under management surpassed NT$300 billion, an annual increase of 77 percent, the bank said.

The bank’s offshore banking unit (OBU) and overseas branches generated combined net profit of NT$4.94 billion in the first 10 months, up 39 percent year-on-year and accounting for 21 percent of the bank’s total earnings.

OBU profit surged 124 percent, as the bank sought to capture growing cross-border financial demand arising from global supply chain restructuring, it said.

Hua Nan Securities Co (華南永昌證券) reported net profit of NT$4.36 billion in the first 10 months, up 163 percent year-on-year, benefiting from increased trading activity and higher turnover in the local stock market.

Growth in underwriting, overseas securities trading and digital financial services also contributed to earnings.

The company’s South China Insurance Co (華南產險) posted net profit of NT$1.75 billion, up 24 percent from a year earlier, supported by stronger underwriting performance and investment returns.

Separately, the company said its digital transformation initiatives had generated more than NT$2 billion in benefits, while AI applications at Hua Nan Bank had delivered productivity gains equivalent to more than NT$200 million in labor costs.

data.title: MiTAC expanding capacity to support business growth
data.description:
MiTAC Holdings Corp (神達控股) yesterday said that continued capacity expansion in Taiwan, Vietnam and the US would help the company meet customers’ diverse needs and boost its business growth next year.

“We have continued expanding our global footprint over the past two years, which means we have sufficient capacity and power supply to support our growth, so we are very positive about next year,” MiTAC Holdings president Billy Ho (何繼武) told an investor conference in Taipei.

MiTAC Holdings counts hyperscalers, cloud service providers, neocloud operators and enterprise customers among its customers. The company has a broader rack-system product portfolio for server, networking, artificial intelligence (AI) compute and storage, Ho said.

Customers are increasingly focused on whether suppliers such as MiTAC Holdings have sufficient liquid-cooling capacity and power availability to support future operations, he said.

The company has relatively low revenue exposure to Southeast Asia and China, with its main markets in the US, Europe and other parts of the Asia-Pacific region, Ho said.

AI regulations and political developments in the US following the midterm elections have a limited impact on the company, he added.

MiTAC Holdings continues to expand capacity in Miaoli County’s Jhunan Township (竹南) and New Taipei City’s Linkou District (林口), with a new plant in Taoyuan’s Yangmei District (楊梅) scheduled for completion in 2028, Ho said.

The company is also constructing new facilities in California’s Newark, San Jose and Fremont, after its Vietnamese plant began operations in March, he said.

The company plans to spend US$500 million to US$600 million in capital expenditure over the next two to three years to further expand capacity in Taiwan, Vietnam and the US, MiTAC Holdings chief financial officer Doris Huang (黃秀玲) said.

MiTAC Holdings comprises MiTAC Computing Technology Corp (神雲科技), MiTAC Digital Technology Corp (神達數位) and MiTAC International Corp (神達電腦).

In the first three quarters of this year, MiTAC Computing accounted for 91.6 percent of MiTAC Holdings’ total revenue of NT$118.12 billion (US$3.59 billion), followed by MiTAC Digital Technology at 6.6 percent and MiTAC International at 1.8 percent.

MiTAC Computing’s rack systems for data centers include AI servers, high-performance computing servers, multi-node servers, graphics processing unit-based servers, general-purpose enterprise servers and storage servers, company president Rick Hwang (黃承德) said.

He said the company has increasingly delivered full-rack systems rather than individual servers as customer demand evolves, with rack solutions tailored to customers’ configurations, including those based on Advanced Micro Devices Inc’s (AMD) Instinct and EPYC processors.

The company expects to roll out its liquid-cooled server racks for AMD’s Helios platform next year, he added.

data.title: Eight banks report NT$1.82 million in unauthorized transfers: FSC
data.description:
Eight banks have reported major incidents involving unauthorized online transfers totaling NT$1.82 million (US$55,201) from the accounts of 10 customers, the Financial Supervisory Commission (FSC) said yesterday.

The eight banks are CTBC Bank Co (中信銀行), E.Sun Commercial Bank Ltd (玉山銀行), Hua Nan Commercial Bank Ltd (華南銀行), Taipei Fubon Commercial Bank Co (台北富邦銀行), Taiwan Cooperative Bank Ltd (合庫銀行), Chang Hwa Commercial Bank Ltd (彰化銀行), First Commercial Bank Ltd (第一銀行) and Taishin International Bank Co (台新銀行), FSC Banking Bureau Secretary-General Chen Chia-chen (陳家珍) said at a news conference.

Separately, the Criminal Investigation Bureau (CIB) said it had received more than 100 reports of unauthorized online banking transfers that occurred between September and Nov. 11. Reported losses totaled NT$17.42 million.

The CIB said 22 financial institutions were affected, including 18 banks, one securities brokerage and three electronic payment providers.

The bureau said it suspected that criminals had used malware hidden in an Android app posing as a short-form video app to take control of users’ phones and transfer money through their mobile banking apps.

Asked about the difference between the two sets of figures, Chen said banks decide whether incidents meet the FSC’s criteria for reporting as major contingencies, while the CIB compiles reports from the public.

In the case involving the securities brokerage, an investor had reported that an order was placed without their knowledge, FSC Securities and Futures Bureau Deputy Director-General Huang Chung-hao (黃仲豪) said.

The brokerage had not reported the incident as a major contingency, but the Taiwan Stock Exchange Corp was looking into it, Huang said. He added that in some cases, investors who suspected their orders had been tampered with later realized they had scheduled the orders themselves.

Asked how customers could seek compensation and whether banks would be held responsible, Chen said the outcome would depend on the circumstances of each case. Customers dissatisfied with the outcome could seek mediation through the Financial Ombudsman Institution, she added.

Chen said the FSC had instructed financial institutions to strengthen their cybersecurity defenses and resilience. In response to the methods described by the CIB, the commission would ask the Bankers Association to discuss ways to improve existing security measures.

The FSC would also work closely with law enforcement agencies and cooperate fully with police investigations, she said.

The commission would ask financial institutions to remind customers to avoid downloading apps from unknown sources or clicking on unfamiliar links, Chen said.

data.title: Fresh tariffs blitz pushes Asian nations to speed up trade deals with Washington
data.description:
US President Donald Trump’s fresh tariff blitz aims to pressure Asian countries into sealing trade deals with Washington to avoid unfavorable duty rates, analysts said yesterday.

The proposed levies announced on Wednesday affect a range of nations in the region. They could result in rates of up to 20 percent on exports from the targeted countries, but face a period of public comment before taking effect, at the earliest in January.

The announcement came after Washington concluded a months-long probe into alleged excess production in the targeted economies.

However, “several of these economies already have prior negotiated tariff rates with the US, which would effectively cap the applicable rate,” Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group Inc economist Lloyd Chan (陳力德) said in a note.

The US has also indicated that the new tolls would not stack on top of other tariffs already imposed on 60 countries over forced labor concerns. Instead, the higher rate would apply.

“In all, that should help contain the incremental tariff shock, assuming prior negotiated commitment remains in place,” Chan said.

However, it does mean that Washington has established higher tariff ceilings that can be activated “should trade negotiations or existing commitments break down,” he added.

Capital Economics Ltd economist Stephen Brown also said that “the US has left open its ability to hike these tariffs if trade agreements fall apart,” particularly with China.

In Beijing’s case, the new levies stand at 20 percent, meaning the total rate could jump to 40 percent if its current trade truce with Washington, set to expire in January, is not extended.

Such a scenario “could take the two largest economies back to the trade wars of 2025,” Atlantic Council international economics chair Josh Lipsky said in a note.

However, that is not something Trump wants, he said.

Instead, Trump is banking on an extension of the truce, although this is “far from a sure thing,” he said.

Other Asian economies, also in Trump’s crosshairs due to significant trade imbalances, are likewise under pressure. Vietnam faces a maximum additional tariff of 35 percent, which could be cut to 20 percent if a trade deal is reached.

Hanoi on Wednesday reiterated that it has made commitments under a framework agreement in October last year, and that it is working for a final deal “as soon as possible.”

India said that trade concerns should be addressed in ongoing talks with Washington for a bilateral trade deal.

The US has proposed a 17 percent rate on Indian goods, rising to a possible 25 percent if no deal is reached.

The countries reached an interim agreement in February aimed at reducing US tariffs on Indian goods.

However, the US Supreme Court struck down Trump’s levies days later, fueling uncertainty over when the agreement would take effect.

In contrast with Indian uncertainty, Taiwan, which reached a deal with Washington early this year, struck a reassuring tone.

“We are confident that when tariffs are finalized early next year, we will return to a 15 percent non-stacked tariff under the agreement between Taiwan and the US,” Vice Premier Cheng Li-chiun (鄭麗君) told a news briefing in Taipei.

data.title: Nvidia halts server sales to 4 SE Asian nations: ‘FT’
data.description:
Nvidia Corp has told manufacturing partners to stop shipping servers containing its chips to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia, the Financial Times (FT) reported yesterday.

The move follows new US curbs that took effect last week, which require export licenses for shipments of advanced chips to several Southeast Asian countries — part of efforts by Washington to shut down routes that Chinese firms are believed to use to obtain advanced artificial intelligence (AI) chips.

Manufacturing partners such as Dell Technologies Inc and Super Micro Computer Inc, which package Nvidia’s chips into servers, told buyers in the four countries that Nvidia would not allow their orders to be shipped, FT reported.

It was unclear whether the halt would be temporary, as Nvidia and its partners work through compliance requirements under new US export controls, the newspaper said, citing three people familiar with the matter.

The US Department of Commerce published the new rule days after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang (黃仁勳) resigned following reports of an affair with a suspected Chinese spy who previously worked at Singapore-based cloud company Megaspeed International Pte.

Nvidia’s board reinstated Huang as CEO on Monday.

Megaspeed, an Nvidia partner that rents computing power at its data centers, has come under scrutiny for possible illegal diversion of advanced AI chips to China.

Separately, S&P Global Ratings is looking at cutting Nvidia’s credit by one notch, citing concerns over the company’s management and governance following the departure, and then the return, of Huang.

“News regarding the CEO and questions regarding potential export control violations have exposed vulnerabilities in Nvidia’s management and governance framework, especially in regard to its board structure, composition, and effectiveness,” S&P said on Wednesday.

The bond grader said it might cut Nvidia’s “AA” rating, the third-highest level, after a 90-day review, known as putting the company on CreditWatch with negative implications.

S&P said it expects that any downgrade would be limited to one notch, unless the company’s future business prospects have been harmed.

S&P’s move comes after its peer, Moody’s Ratings, last week lowered Nvidia’s outlook to stable from positive, also citing governance concerns after Huang’s ouster.

The shift in outlook means that Nvidia’s “Aa1” credit grade, the second-highest investment-grade rating, is unlikely to get a boost over the next 12 to 18 months, Moody’s said in a statement.

On Wednesday, Moody’s kept its outlook unchanged, saying “governance and regulatory uncertainty remains” following Additional reporting by Bloomberg

data.title: Netherlands plans to fight rollout of proposed US curbs on ASML
data.description:
The Dutch government said it will resist US plans to further restrict ASML Holding NV’s sales to China, calling the proposed rules a threat to Europe’s most valuable company.

The US’ Multilateral Alignment of Technology Controls on Hardware (MATCH) Act, which aims to keep semiconductor components away from China, would force the Netherlands and other allies to strengthen export controls on advanced equipment, including Veldhoven, Netherlands-based ASML’s chipmaking machines.

The Dutch government is opposed to the extraterritorial scope of the bill, Dutch Minister of Foreign Trade and Development Cooperation Sjoerd Sjoerdsma said in parliament yesterday.

“The US is not the boss of Veldhoven,” Sjoerdsma said. “The US has a certain amount of jealousy of the capacities that the Netherlands and ASML have here — they would really like to have that within their own borders, but they don’t. In a good partnership, we would both be able to profit from that, but it’s not an equal partnership now.”

Sjoerdsma’s comments mark an escalation in rhetoric after months of Dutch efforts to prevent the MATCH Act from passing. The Dutch government is lobbying to make sure the act isn’t attached to an upcoming US defense bill, because the act would be less likely to pass on its own. ASML is the only company that makes the lithography machines used to manufacture cutting-edge semiconductors for artificial intelligence data centers and advanced smartphones.

While ASML has never been allowed to ship its most advanced extreme ultraviolet (EUV) machines to China, the Match Act is expected to expand those restrictions to impact sales and servicing of ASML’s immersion lithography, or immersion deep ultraviolet (DUV), machines to China. China is one of the chip-equipment maker’s biggest markets and is expected to account for about a fifth of revenue this year.

“If it does get passed, we’ll do everything we can to prevent it from being implemented,” Sjoerdsma said, declining to be specific about the Dutch government’s potential response. “And if it is implemented, we’ll really have to consider how we’re going to respond. But there’s a lot on the table for the Dutch cabinet.”

Sjoerdsma also said the detrimental effects would not be felt in the Netherlands alone, and other European countries’ semiconductor industries would also be hit.

“The consequences will be felt throughout the European Union, also as it will create a strong precedent,” Sjoerdsma said.

“Europe can’t afford to fall behind,” he said in a reference to the importance of the semiconductor industry and the rapid developments in AI.

Sjoerdsma said he was working with the European Commission, Germany and France in an effort to prevent the MATCH Act from being attached to the defense bill.

In case that lobbying fails, the Netherlands and the EU will weigh their options to limit the consequences, he said.

Additional reporting by Reuters

data.title: US chip curbs, distillation crackdown threaten Chinese AI model development, sources say
data.description:
China’s Z.AI Co (智譜) has fallen behind schedule on its next flagship artificial intelligence (AI) model, while rival Moonshot AI Technology Co (月之暗面) expects the interval between major releases could double from six months to a year or longer if it loses access to overseas computing power, people familiar with the matter said.

The previously unreported details show how efforts by US AI companies OpenAI and Anthropic PBC to prevent distillation, a technique in which developers train models using answers generated by more capable ones, have slowed Chinese AI development. Washington’s latest chip restrictions threaten further delays.

The measures jeopardize a key advantage that has helped Chinese AI companies challenge their American rivals despite years of export controls: the ability to develop competitive models at substantially lower cost.

A US Department of Commerce rule that took effect on Nov. 19 imposes licensing requirements aimed at restricting Chinese companies’ access to large amounts of computing power from advanced US chips in overseas data centers, targeting a means of accessing Nvidia Corp processors without importing them.

Z.AI, also known as Zhipu AI, had planned to release its next flagship model, GLM-5.5, this month but has yet to do so, two people familiar with the matter said on condition of anonymity.

The model, designed with roughly 3 trillion parameters - a measure of its size - has been held up partly by increasingly effective safeguards against distillation, one of the people said.

Z.AI had hoped to complete training and release the model by year-end, but the new US computing restrictions could push its launch into the first quarter of next year or later, the person said.

On Monday, the company released GLM-5.4, built on an existing model with 750 billion parameters. Z.AI says a new design enables it to match the performance of models with 2 trillion to 3 trillion parameters.

Anthropic said in September it had observed nearly 200 million exchanges with its Claude models linked to suspected distillation campaigns, attributing them to Chinese developers including Alibaba Group Holding Ltd (阿里巴巴), Moonshot and Z.AI.

OpenAI has made similar accusations against individuals associated with Moonshot. Anthropic has described measures it uses to detect and block unauthorised distillation, while OpenAI has also reported efforts to disrupt such activity.

LONGER DEVELOPMENT CYCLES

Beijing-based Moonshot is particularly exposed to the new US rule because it rents computing power to train its models and prioritizes overseas providers, a person with knowledge of its operations said.

The AI developer internally expects its usual six-month interval between major releases could stretch to 12 months or longer if its overseas computing access is cut off entirely, the person said, adding that computing capacity available in China could not make up the shortfall.

Its next flagship model, Kimi K4, could be delayed until around the middle of next year, the person estimated. Moonshot released Kimi K2 in July last year, K2.5 in January and K3 in July.

Moonshot has stepped up efforts to rent computing power in Europe, a separate person familiar with the matter said, confirming an earlier CNBC report. It plans to approach Chinese chipmakers about using their processors for training, the person added.

Safeguards against distillation have also slowed Moonshot’s development, the person said. As obtaining training data from Anthropic’s and OpenAI’s models has become increasingly difficult, Moonshot has begun distilling from models developed by Google and Meta Platforms Inc, whose latest releases have made them attractive sources of training data, the person added.

CLOSING THE CHIP LOOPHOLE

The new US restrictions on overseas data centres followed the short-lived resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang (黃仁勳) over revelations of extramarital affairs. The rule covers computing arrangements at data centres outside the US above a threshold roughly equivalent to 750 of Nvidia’s H100 chips, which have required US export licences for shipments to China since 2022.

Operators already providing covered computing services before the rule took effect have 90 days to obtain licences.

It also introduces licensing requirements for shipments of advanced chips, including H100s, to Malaysia, Singapore, Indonesia, Thailand and Brazil, with exceptions for qualifying US companies.

data.title: Business sentiment cautious: TIER
data.description:
VISIBILITY SUBDUED: The more cautious sentiment does not necessarily signal deterioration in growth, an economist said, urging investors to wait and see

Taiwanese business sentiment turned slightly more cautious about the economic outlook as uncertainty over US politics and the prospect of US Federal Reserve rate hikes clouded expectations for export orders and investment next year, despite robust demand for artificial intelligence (AI), the Taiwan Institute of Economic Research (TIER, 台灣經濟研究院) said yesterday.

The institute’s composite index for the manufacturing sector fell 2.85 points to 98.94 last month, and that for the service sector dropped 2.09 points to 90.13, while the construction index edged up to 109.39, highlighting diverging conditions across sectors.

“Uncertainty over US policies following the midterm elections and financial market pressure from further Federal Reserve rate increases are the two biggest concerns,” TIER economist Gordon Sun (孫明德) told a news conference in Taipei.

Businesses are watching whether export orders can sustain their strong momentum and whether political developments in the US would disrupt investment in AI infrastructure, Sun said.

The more cautious sentiment does not necessarily signal deterioration in economic growth prospects, he said, urging businesses and investors to adopt a wait-and-see approach rather than becoming overly concerned.

Manufacturing sentiment remains supported by robust global demand for AI computing power, Sun said.

Although tighter reviews of data-center projects by some US states could slow the development of new facilities, most projects scheduled to begin operations next year are already in the construction phase, the TIER said.

That should sustain near-term demand for AI hardware and keep capacity utilization high at Taiwanese wafer foundries, advanced packaging facilities and high-end testing providers, the institute said.

Meanwhile, the service sector faces a different mix of pressures, it said, adding that department store anniversary sales and holiday spending provided support for retailers, but financial market volatility weighed on financial services providers.

Expectations of further US rate increases, concerns over rising debt among cloud service providers and a sharp technology stock selloff contributed to a decline in the TAIEX last month. The downturn in the stock market also pushed securities firms’ proprietary trading operations into losses, the TIER said.

Construction businesses remained relatively optimistic about the six-month outlook, supported by technology-related factory projects and higher government infrastructure spending planned for next year, despite labor shortages and elevated costs for building materials and earthwork disposal, TIER Taiwan Industry Economics Database director Arisa Liu (劉佩真) said.

However, the residential property market is expected to remain subdued, as Taiwan’s central bank is unlikely to broadly relax credit restrictions, while mortgage rates remain elevated, and banks continue to face competing demands for lending funds, she said.

Housing demand next year is likely to be driven mainly by owner-occupiers, with the market expected to go through a period of consolidation before staging a modest recovery, she added.
